title: Implementing AI-assisted, patient-friendly imaging report summaries to enhance oncology care delivery: protocol for a randomized mixed-methods quality improvement study
authors: Ryan Baumann, M.; Barton, H. J.; Voorheis, P.; Dahl, C.; DuBenske, L.; Commers, W.; Mast, K.; Campbell, T.; Patterson, B. W.; Emamekhoo, H.
abstract: BackgroundAs required by the 21st Century Cures Act, all test results, including final radiology reports, are released to patients as soon as the results are finalized. However, radiology reports are primarily intended for communication between medical professionals and can often be difficult for patients to interpret, particularly in cancer care settings. We developed a tool that leverages a large language model (LLM; ChatGPT-5.2, OpenAI, San Francisco, CA) to draft a patient-friendly plain language version of imaging results (Patient-Friendly Scan Result Generation [PFSG] tool) that oncologists can incorporate into their communication with patients via patient portals. This article describes our mixed-methods study protocol. ObjectiveOur primary aims are to: 1) assess whether patients who receive patient-friendly versions of scan results report better understanding of their results than patients who do not; 2) assess whether introduction of the PFSG tool affects provider workload; and 3) explain how and under what circumstances the PFSG tool enhances communication and workflows, and affects patient and provider outcomes. MethodsWe will use an embedded mixed-methods, prospective cohort design within a quality improvement (QI) initiative. The PFSG tool will be implemented using a modified three-wave staircase trial design, with providers in randomized cohorts of oncology disease groups progressively gaining access to the tool over the course of the study. Approximately 60 providers from 11 oncology disease focus groups will be randomized. Longitudinal provider outcomes will be measured through surveys at one month pre-implementation, one month post-implementation, and three months post-implementation. Patient outcomes will be measured cross-sectionally through surveys at one month pre-implementation (n=350) and at post-implementation result point-of-contact (n=350). Additionally, we will conduct interviews with patients and oncologists to inform the iterative design of the tool and its implementation. ResultsThis study was funded in September 2025 and data collection began in February 2026. As of September 2026, the PFSG tool has been rolled out to all oncology providers, with Cohort 3 post-implementation data collection beginning in August 2026. A total of 738 patient baseline surveys have been collected and patient post-implementation data collection is in progress. ConclusionsThis is the protocol for a study of the implementation of a patient-friendly results tool in oncology provider workflows to facilitate improved communication of radiology results to oncology patients. The results of this study will lend evidence to the utility and acceptability of the study tool, and tools like it, to close an important oncology care gap. If the tool is shown to improve key oncology patient and provider outcomes, it may lead to development of a wider release for more general patient populations. Trial Registrationhttps://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07532083

infographic.key_insight: Researchers are testing an AI tool that turns radiology results into plain-language summaries so oncology patients may better understand their scan findings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: If effective, the tool could improve patient communication in cancer care without adding substantial burden for oncology teams.
method: Embedded mixed-methods QI study with a randomized three-wave staircase rollout across oncology disease groups
About 60 providers from 11 disease focus groups plus two patient survey cohorts (350 pre-implementation, 350 post-implementation)
Provider surveys at 1 month pre-, 1 month post-, and 3 months post-implementation, plus patient and oncologist interviews
infographic.evidence_signal: This is a protocol paper, so the abstract reports planned surveys, interviews, and rollout evaluation rather than outcome results.
infographic.watch_item: AI-generated summaries will need careful oversight to avoid inaccuracies, over-simplification, or workflow friction in real-world oncology messaging.
infographic.paper_title: Implementing AI-assisted, patient-friendly imaging report summaries to enhance oncology care delivery: protocol for a randomized mixed-methods quality improvement study

title: Large language model consensus for reliable research cohort construction from radiology reports: a retrospective cohort study
authors: Rui, W.; Ma, J.; Stepanov, V.; Bunnell, A.; Lan, M.; Chen, J.; Patel, R. R.; Novikov, D. S.; Fieremans, E.; Shen, Y.
abstract: BackgroundLarge-scale retrospective studies often require researchers to adjudicate outcomes or cohort eligibility from unstructured clinical records. Manual review can provide reliable labels but is difficult to scale. We developed and evaluated a consensus workflow using multiple large language models (LLMs) to automatically assign high-confidence outcome labels while deferring ambiguous cases for manual review. MethodsWe included 6,718 brain MRI reports from 5,856 patients. The expert-adjudicated reference set included 680 reports from 675 patients: 372 normal (age-appropriate without significant intracranial pathology), 90 white matter hyperintensity-only (WMH-only; isolated nonspecific WMHs potentially ambiguous for binary classification), and 218 abnormal (other intracranial pathology) reports. We evaluated proprietary-inclusive (Qwen3/Kimi-Linear/GPT-5) and open-source (Qwen3/Kimi-Linear/DeepSeek-R1) ensembles against individual LLMs. Ensembles assigned a normal or abnormal label only when all models agreed; all other reports were classified as uncertain and deferred for manual review. Individual LLMs assigned normal or abnormal predictions and classified WMH-only predictions as uncertain. In the full cohort, we compared the prevalence of active central nervous system (CNS)-related International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) diagnoses across the normal, uncertain, and abnormal groups generated by each ensemble. ResultsIn the expert-adjudicated reference set, both ensembles achieved 100% precision for automatically assigned normal and abnormal reports. GPT-5 was the strongest individual LLM but had lower precision than either ensemble, with normal and abnormal precision of 98.9% and 94.1%, respectively, and 17 expert-label mismatches versus none for the consensus ensembles. In the full cohort, 1.6% of reports classified as normal were associated with CNS-related ICD-10 diagnoses, compared with 29.7% of uncertain and 51.3% of abnormal reports for the proprietary-inclusive ensemble; corresponding rates were 1.6%, 31.1%, and 51.6% for the open-source ensemble. ConclusionsRequiring unanimous agreement across multiple LLMs enabled high-precision automatic adjudication while directing ambiguous cases to manual review. This strategy may reduce the burden of manual adjudication and support scalable construction of high-purity research cohorts from unstructured clinical text.

infographic.key_insight: A unanimous multi-LLM consensus workflow can automatically label clearly normal or abnormal radiology reports with very high precision while routing ambiguous cases to manual review.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could help researchers build large retrospective cohorts from radiology reports faster and with less expert review, while preserving reliability for uncertain findings.
method: Reviewed 6,718 brain MRI reports from 5,856 patients.
Used two LLM ensembles: proprietary-inclusive and open-source; a report was auto-labeled only if all models agreed.
Reports with disagreement, including WMH-only cases, were marked uncertain and deferred to manual review.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a 680-report expert-adjudicated reference set, both ensembles reached 100% precision for automatically assigned normal and abnormal labels, and the uncertain group was enriched for CNS-related ICD-10 diagnoses.
infographic.watch_item: High precision came with more deferred cases, so implementation depends on available manual-review capacity and may vary outside brain MRI report settings.
infographic.paper_title: Large language model consensus for reliable research cohort construction from radiology reports: a retrospective cohort study

title: Machine Learning Models Using Electronic Health Record Data to Predict Obstructive Sleep Apnea
authors: Hwang, N. H.; Mazzotti, D. R.; Mishra, S.; Westover, M. B.; Hwang, D.; Thomas, R. J.; Mignot, E.; Katwa, U.; Shi, J. M.; Yan, R.; Becker, K. A.; Klimper, M. T.; Jara, J.; Stevens, D. R.; Gratton, M. K. P.; Sun, H.
abstract: RationaleObstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is highly prevalent yet largely under-diagnosed. Current screening strategies rely on effortful questionnaires with modest accuracy, and prior machine learning models often require resource-intensive inputs and lack external validation. ObjectivesTo develop and validate machine learning models to predict OSA (apnea-hypopnea index [AHI4%][≥]5) and moderate-severe OSA (AHI4%[≥]15) using only routinely collected electronic health record (EHR) data, test cross-system transferability and compare performance with clinical screeners and a Bayesian risk-updating framework. MethodsThree tree-ensemble families (XGBoost, random forests, and histogram-based gradient boosting) were trained on an adult cohort with sleep-study results at Kaiser Permanente (KPSC), using full (106-feature) and minimal (age, sex, body-mass index, race/ethnicity) predictor sets and tuned by nested cross-validation. XGBoost models were selected, internally and temporally validated, and externally validated at University of Kansas Medical Center (KUMC). Measurements and Main ResultsOn our internal hold-out set (n=53,048), the full XGBoost model reached a ROC-AUC of 0.791 for any OSA and 0.768 for moderate-severe OSA. The minimal model retained most performance (0.764 and 0.736). Temporal performance was stable. Externally, frozen models showed lower AUCs (0.718 and 0.690 for full models; 0.725 and 0.706 for minimal models) but similar to KUMC-native models and improved further with transfer learning. The models significantly outperformed STOP-BANG (AUC difference 0.06-0.09 for predicting any OSA; p<0.001). Bayesian updating with select patient-reported items further improved discrimination. ConclusionsMachine learning models based on EHR data can predict OSA probability that outperform existing screeners, transfers across systems, and offers potential for EHR implementation. At a Glance CommentaryO_ST_ABSScientific Knowledge on the SubjectC_ST_ABSObstructive sleep apnea is common and heavily underdiagnosed, yet upstream patient identification still depends on symptom and anthropometry questionnaires such as STOP-BANG, which are effort-dependent and achieve modest performance. Prior machine learning models for OSA are heterogeneous, often developed on small or demographically narrow cohorts, frequently rely on physiologic signals that reintroduce a testing step, and are rarely validated across independent health systems. What This Study Adds to the FieldWe developed machine learning models from routinely collected electronic health record data, comprising a full (106-feature) and a minimal (4-feature) model, to predict any OSA and moderate-severe OSA. The study is distinguished by multiple validation efforts, including temporal validation and external validation at a second health system. We further explored adaptation strategies for external adoption using transfer learning techniques. Finally, the models outperformed existing screeners such as STOP-BANG, and we describe a Bayesian framework that optionally incorporates select patient-reported symptoms to refine individual risk estimates. Overall, these models are feasible to implement within EHR systems as a low-effort, passive screener that can support encounter-based and population health outreach screening strategies.

infographic.key_insight: Routine electronic health record data can predict obstructive sleep apnea with moderate accuracy, and a minimal model using age, sex, BMI, and race/ethnicity performed nearly as well as a full-feature model.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could support earlier OSA risk flagging inside health systems and may outperform common screening questionnaires like STOP-BANG.
method: Trained tree-ensemble machine learning models on Kaiser Permanente EHR data with sleep-study outcomes.
Compared full 106-feature and minimal 4-feature predictor sets using nested cross-validation.
Validated internally, temporally, and externally at University of Kansas Medical Center, with transfer-learning experiments and comparison to clinical screeners.
infographic.evidence_signal: On an internal hold-out set, the full XGBoost model achieved ROC-AUC 0.791 for any OSA and 0.768 for moderate-severe OSA, with external AUCs around 0.69-0.73 and performance above STOP-BANG.
infographic.watch_item: External performance dropped versus internal testing, so real-world deployment will need careful calibration, site-specific validation, and attention to data differences across health systems.
infographic.paper_title: Machine Learning Models Using Electronic Health Record Data to Predict Obstructive Sleep Apnea

title: Large Language Models for Structured Information Extraction from German Histopathology Reports - Hepatocellular Carcinoma
authors: Koch, N.; Hartmann, N.; Maennel, A.; Baretton, G.; Aust, D.; Hoenscheid, P.
abstract: Background: Clinical registries and institutional quality control (QC) in pathology heavily depend on complex histopathological data. However, critical tumor characteristics are mostly locked in unstructured free-text reports. We hypothesize that locally deployed, resource-efficient language models operating within a secure institutional network can reliably extract relevant variables from German reports of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), thereby enabling automated data curation without transferring sensitive patient data. Methods: We developed a local, privacy-preserving open-weight Large Language Model (LLM) pipeline consisting of two consecutive stages: Stage 1 utilizes a lightweight gatekeeper model to isolate the target cohort of confirmed Hepatocellular Carcinoma cases from a screening pool of N = 2,864 reports. Stage 2 deploys a high-capacity model to extract 15 predefined histopathological variables, including tumor-node-metastasis staging, histological grading, vascular invasion, and selected immunohistochemical features into structured JSON format. For both Stages, pipeline performance was evaluated using Accuracy, Macro F1-scores, and Cohen's kappa compared to expert-curated reference annotations. Results: The top-performing Stage 1 gatekeeper isolated the target patient cohort with zero classification errors, effectively reaching complete agreement with the reference standard (ground truth) and correcting inaccurate administrative metadata. For Stage 2 feature extraction, current-generation models demonstrated robust structural reliability, reducing the burden of manual post-processing. The 31B model configuration (Gemma 4) virtually eliminated objective factual errors, achieving near-perfect agreement with the reference standard (Macro F1 > 0.99). Conclusion: Local two-stage pipelines offer a highly accurate, resource-efficient, and secure solution for clinical text processing. This framework serves as a privacy-preserving engine for institutional quality control and the scalable curation of pathology registries.

infographic.key_insight: A local two-stage language model pipeline can accurately find hepatocellular carcinoma cases and extract structured histopathology variables from German free-text reports.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could support privacy-preserving registry curation and pathology quality control without sending sensitive patient data outside the institution.
method: Stage 1: a lightweight gatekeeper model screened 2,864 reports to identify confirmed HCC cases.
Stage 2: a higher-capacity model extracted 15 predefined variables into JSON, including staging, grade, vascular invasion, and immunohistochemistry.
All processing ran locally within a secure institutional network.
infographic.evidence_signal: The best pipeline showed zero classification errors in cohort detection and near-perfect extraction performance, with the 31B Gemma 4 model reporting Macro F1 > 0.99 against expert reference annotations.
infographic.watch_item: Performance was measured on expert-curated reference data, so real-world deployment still needs checks for unseen report styles, rare edge cases, and ongoing quality monitoring.
infographic.paper_title: Large Language Models for Structured Information Extraction from German Histopathology Reports - Hepatocellular Carcinoma

title: HealthFound: a health world model for quantitative reasoning on longitudinal health profiles
authors: Guo, H.; Song, L.; Ren, P.; Han, J.; Wang, Y.; Li, H.; Deng, J.; Wang, J.; Gong, W.; Feng, J.; Cheng, W.
abstract: Medical large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in medical knowledge retrieval and clinical reasoning. However, their capacity for quantitative reasoning over dense, longitudinal health data remains limited, largely due to the lack of effective training strategies that leverage large-scale, natural-language-based prospective cohorts. To address this, we present HealthFound, a medical LLM trained on 12.4 million self-constructed examples. These include 15-year longitudinal biomedical records from 501,936 participants, as well as datasets for medical knowledge and general reasoning. We propose a novel three-stage training framework comprising progressive curriculum supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampled retention fine-tuning, and task-verifiable policy optimization. This enables the model to effectively parse heterogeneous quantitative follow-up data and perform robust quantitative reasoning. HealthFound achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple newly constructed benchmarks. It attains the highest accuracy on eight public medical benchmarks for general medical competence. On 1,162 UK Biobank tasks predicting future disease onset from biomedical measurements, it outperforms the second-best model by over 10 percentage points on average. In two independent external validations (MIMIC-IV and NHANES), it demonstrates superior zero-shot generalization, achieving improvements of over 6% across 484 disease endpoints. The model also achieves top results on novel tasks for literature-derived question answering and quantitative indicator imputation. Furthermore, HealthFound generates interpretable reasoning rationales that are consistent with established biomedical knowledge. Collectively, our results demonstrate that HealthFound enables medical LLMs to evolve from static knowledge repositories into dynamic quantitative reasoning engines over longitudinal health data.

infographic.key_insight: HealthFound is a medical LLM designed to reason quantitatively over long-term patient data, turning longitudinal health records into actionable predictive reasoning.
infographic.clinical_relevance: It may help support earlier disease risk prediction and more robust interpretation of complex follow-up measurements in clinical and research settings.
method: Trained on 12.4 million examples, including 15-year longitudinal biomedical records from 501,936 participants.
Used a three-stage pipeline: progressive curriculum supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampled retention fine-tuning, and task-verifiable policy optimization.
Combined cohort data with medical knowledge and general reasoning tasks to improve quantitative reasoning.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was evaluated on 1,162 UK Biobank prediction tasks, eight public medical benchmarks, and external validations in MIMIC-IV and NHANES, with reported gains of 6%+ across 484 disease endpoints.
infographic.watch_item: Because the model is trained and tested on complex retrospective datasets, real-world deployment would still need careful validation for bias, calibration, and workflow fit.
infographic.paper_title: HealthFound: a health world model for quantitative reasoning on longitudinal health profiles

title: Forecasting Alzheimer's disease progression using non-imaging clinical features and XGBoost
authors: Gautier, A.; Zheng, L.; Schreurs, B. G.
abstract: Identifying progressive dementia during its prodromal stage is a challenging yet critical task for healthcare providers. Traditional clinical assessments are often not sensitive enough to detect warning signs of cognitive decline. Machine learning (ML) methods have shown promise in modeling clinical trajectories associated with neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimers disease (AD). Validation of these models forecasting abilities, however, is widely lacking in the literature. To address this gap, we established a longitudinal cohort from the National Alzheimers Coordinating Center (n = 15,727) comprising individuals who were cognitively normal (CN) or had mild cognitive impairment (MCI) at baseline. Cognitive status and clinical observations collected over up to 10 visits were used to train several ML classifiers. We employed the gradient-boosted tree ensemble method XGBoost with a custom feature-engineering pipeline. On non-imputed data, our models achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.9447 [0.9417-0.9476] and PR-AUC of 0.8554 [0.8497-0.8611] for the CN[->]MCI task, and an AUC-ROC of 0.9059 [0.8983-0.9134] and PR-AUC of 0.9214 [0.9156-0.9272] for the MCI[->]AD task. In a lead-time forecasting analysis spanning mean follow-up periods of 56.1 months (range, 9.1-214.1) for CN[->]MCI and 42.7 months (range, 9.1-126.1) for MCI[->]AD, the non-imputed models detected future progression before diagnosis in 29.58% [28.29%-30.87%] of CN[->]MCI progressors and 22.41% [21.36%-23.46%] of MCI[->]AD progressors. Among these individuals, the mean lead time was 33.04 months [32.52-33.56] and 17.95 months [17.71-18.19], respectively. False alarm rates among non-progressors were 12.6% [11.5%-13.7%] and 20.0% [18.4%-21.6%], respectively. These findings suggest that longitudinal machine learning models can identify future cognitive decline before diagnosis, indicating clinical utility for early dementia risk stratification. Author summaryAlzheimers disease (AD) is a progressive and currently incurable neurodegenerative disorder that remains highly difficult to diagnose during its early stages. While modern early-stage dementia research relies on advanced neuroimaging, the high cost of these tests excludes many vulnerable communities. We designed our study to advance scalable, low-cost diagnostic alternatives that can identify individuals at significant risk of cognitive decline, ensuring faster access to emerging therapies. We examined trajectories of cognitive decline in 15,727 adults (mean age = 71.45 years, SD = 9.06) who had between 2 and 10 follow-up visits. Using 37 demographic, behavioral, clinical, and genetic variables, we modeled cognitively stable and declining trajectories using the XGBoost algorithm. Additionally, we evaluated the models ability to forecast future diagnoses and the impact of longitudinal imputation. Our models performed well in both classification tasks (AUC-ROC [≥] 0.90). Imputation did not substantively alter the classifiers performance. In forecasting diagnosis conversion, the models raised alarms before the recorded conversion visit in a subset of progressors, with non-imputed models yielding longer net lead times than imputed models in AD forecasting. This work describes a strategy for handling mixed-length temporal dimensions in longitudinal cohorts and evaluates its prognostic ability.

infographic.key_insight: A longitudinal XGBoost model using non-imaging clinical features can forecast future Alzheimer’s-related cognitive decline before formal diagnosis.
infographic.clinical_relevance: If validated further, this approach could support earlier dementia risk stratification using routinely collected clinical data rather than imaging alone.
method: National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center cohort of 15,727 participants who were cognitively normal or had MCI at baseline
Longitudinal clinical and cognitive features from up to 10 visits were engineered into XGBoost classifiers
Two progression tasks were modeled: CN→MCI and MCI→AD
infographic.evidence_signal: On non-imputed data, performance was strong (CN→MCI AUC-ROC 0.9447, PR-AUC 0.8554; MCI→AD AUC-ROC 0.9059, PR-AUC 0.9214), with detectable lead time before diagnosis in a subset of progressors.
infographic.watch_item: The results come from retrospective cohort data, so real-world prospective validation and calibration across clinics are still needed before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Forecasting Alzheimer's disease progression using non-imaging clinical features and XGBoost

title: Assessment of Fairness and Bias of an Image-based Surgical Site Infection Detection AI Model
authors: Lee, F. G.; Choudhary, A.; Li-Han, L. Y.; Dale, E. L.; Bankes, A. C.; Varghese, C.; Anderson, S. S.; Habermann, E. B.; Etzioni, D. A.; McLaughlin, S. A.; Salehinejad, H.; Thiels, C. A.
abstract: BackgroundEvaluating fairness in artificial intelligence (AI) is essential before clinical implementation to prevent unintended harm across diverse patient populations. This study assesses performance differences of an image-based surgical site infection (SSI) detection model across age, gender, geography, race, and skin color. MethodsModel development/validation study using retrospective, multicenter data across surgical subspecialties from adults who submitted an image of their incision via the electronic health record within 30 days of their procedure between 2019-2024. Area under receiver operating curve (AUROC) was compared by age (<55 vs. [≥]55 years old), gender (male vs. female), geography (Rochester, Minnesota vs. Jacksonville, Florida vs. Scottsdale, Arizona vs. regional Minnesota/Wisconsin areas), race (White/Caucasian vs. non-White/Caucasian), and skin color (Fitpatrick I-III vs. IV-VI and Monk A-E vs. F-J). ResultsTraining data contained 13,702 images from 4,274 patients between 2019-2022 (50.1% [≥]55 years old; 63.2% female; 91.6% White/Caucasian; 58.5% Rochester, 17.3% Florida, 10.5% Arizona; 96.3% light skin tone), of which 1,348 images (9.8%) had an SSI. No differences in SSI detection existed for age, gender, race, or skin color (AUROC 0.83-0.87, p>0.09), however geographical differences were significant: lowest AUROC 0.83 (95% CI 0.77-0.88) vs. highest AUROC 0.87 (95% CI 0.84-0.89, p=0.01). Temporal validation using 4,242 images from 1,353 patients between 2022-2023 showed intact fairness across subgroups ({Delta}AUROC [≤]0.06) except geography ({Delta}AUROC [≤]0.16). ConclusionsThe model behaved fairly across age, gender, race, and skin color, however geographical differences persisted. These findings have practical implications underscoring the importance of evaluating bias in clinical AI before deployment.

infographic.key_insight: The SSI detection AI model showed similar performance across age, gender, race, and skin color, but performance varied by geography.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This suggests the model may be broadly fair for several demographic groups, yet site-specific differences should be checked before clinical use.
method: Retrospective multicenter development and validation study using adult incision images submitted through the EHR within 30 days after surgery.
Compared AUROC across age, gender, geography, race, and skin color subgroups.
Used both internal training data and temporal validation to assess fairness over time.
infographic.evidence_signal: Training used 13,702 images from 4,274 patients and validation used 4,242 images from 1,353 patients; AUROC was 0.83-0.87 overall, with geography showing the only significant differences.
infographic.watch_item: The dataset was heavily skewed toward White and light-skin-tone patients, so fairness conclusions may be less certain for underrepresented groups and new hospital settings.
infographic.paper_title: Assessment of Fairness and Bias of an Image-based Surgical Site Infection Detection AI Model

title: Considerations for implementing a machine learning model for suicide risk in the health systems that serve American Indian communities
authors: Dayal, R. R.; Goklish, N. A.; Adams, R.; Rebman, P.; Suttle, R.; Garcia, M.; Mega, J.; de la Sierra, V. Q.; Haroz, E. E.
abstract: ObjectiveWe explored the implementation considerations of machine learning (ML) suicide risk identification in a health system that serves primarily American Indian patients in the Southwestern United States. Previous work developed and reported the performance of suicide risk models, but traditional performance metrics do not directly reflect clinical workflows. Materials and MethodsUsing EHR data collected for Emergency Department (ED) visits between 10/01/2019 and 10/02/2021, we conducted Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) to identify the standardized net benefit (SNB) of all models previously evaluated and plotted the potential workload implications of the model with the greatest SNB. Finally, we evaluated suicide screening practices during the study period to inform implementation barriers. ResultsAmong 9,244 patients, 139 (1.5%) had a suicide attempt or death within 90 days of an included visit. The population-specific logistic regression model had the greatest SNB compared to other approaches. When operationalized, the 95th percentile cutoff did not substantially increase clinical workloads, while the 75th percentile cutoff substantially impacted workloads. The secondary analysis on suicide screening depicted variations in screening administration over time. DiscussionWhile DCA identified advantages of ML suicide risk identification over current standards, the complexities of suicide-related care limited its clinical interpretability. A stepped-care framework may mitigate potential workload burdens. Training initiatives and dynamic implementation strategies will support high-quality implementation of ML suicide risk identification. ConclusionOur analyses support the feasibility and utility of augmenting existing suicide screening practices with ML suicide risk identification, and demonstrate the importance of nuanced analyses to inform implementation considerations.

infographic.key_insight: A population-specific machine learning model showed the best decision-curve benefit for identifying suicide risk in a health system serving primarily American Indian patients, with workload depending strongly on the alert threshold.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This suggests ML could augment existing suicide screening in emergency care, but implementation should be designed to fit local workflows and staffing capacity.
method: EHR data from ED visits between 10/01/2019 and 10/02/2021 were analyzed.
Decision Curve Analysis was used to compare standardized net benefit across previously developed models.
Potential workload impact was estimated for the best-performing model, and screening practices were reviewed over time.
infographic.evidence_signal: In 9,244 patients, 139 (1.5%) had a suicide attempt or death within 90 days; the population-specific logistic regression model had the highest standardized net benefit, and a 95th-percentile cutoff had limited workload impact compared with a 75th-percentile cutoff.
infographic.watch_item: Suicide-related care is operationally complex, so model performance may not translate cleanly into real-world screening and alert workflows.
infographic.paper_title: Considerations for implementing a machine learning model for suicide risk in the health systems that serve American Indian communities

title: External Evaluation and Calibration Drift of Explainable Machine Learning Models for Acute and Chronic GVHD Prediction After Allogeneic HSCT
authors: Syed, N.; Ahmed, N.; Abuhaleeqa, M.; Al Kaabi, F. M.; Raza, A.; Al Zaki, A.; Sammour, F.; Alkhatib, Y.; Gopalakrishnan, D.; Afrooz, I.; Damlaj, M.; Abu Jazar, H.; Abdel-Razeq, H.; Halahleh, K.; Yaqub, M.; Hashmi, S.
abstract: ObjectivesMachine learning models for graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) are rarely evaluated externally or for calibration. We developed explainable models for grade II-IV acute and moderate-to-severe chronic GVHD and evaluated their transportability across multiple cohorts. Materials and methodsGradient boosting models were trained on three CIBMTR registry-derived datasets (N = 2,509) and externally evaluated in six cohorts (N = 14,788), including a Middle Eastern cohort. We assessed discrimination (AUROC), calibration (logistic recalibration intercept and slope; Brier score), and SHAP feature explanations. ResultsInternal discrimination was higher for chronic (AUROC 0.736) than acute GVHD (0.624); chronic calibration was good (intercept +0.258, slope 1.073), whereas the acute model was underdispersed (slope 1.802). Externally, the chronic model retained modest, above-chance discrimination (AUROC 0.54-0.64), whereas acute performance fell toward chance (0.52-0.57). Calibration drifted unpredictably, overestimating risk in 9 of 10 evaluable cohort-outcome combinations (intercepts -0.78 to +0.15; slopes 0.12 to 1.98; Brier 0.23-0.27). DiscussionRoutine registry variables carry a transportable signal for chronic GVHD, but acute GVHD likely requires additional biological or clinical predictors. Neither the direction nor the magnitude of calibration drift could be anticipated from training performance. ConclusionInternal performance does not guarantee external utility. Cohort-specific recalibration and routine calibration reporting are required before any clinical use; this study offers a reusable template for multi-cohort external evaluation of clinical prediction models. Lay SummaryAfter a stem cell transplant from a donor, the donors immune cells can attack the patients body, a complication called graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). It can appear early (acute) or months later (chronic), and knowing who is at highest risk before transplant could help doctors plan prevention and follow-up. We built computer models that estimate GVHD risk using information routinely recorded at transplant, trained them on 2,509 patients from a large US transplant registry, and then tested them on six other groups totalling almost 15,000 patients, including patients from the United Arab Emirates and Jordan. The model for chronic GVHD kept a modest ability to separate higher-from lower-risk patients in every group, but the model for acute GVHD performed little better than chance outside the data it was built on. In almost every new group, both models overestimated how many patients would develop GVHD, by amounts that could not be predicted in advance. This shows that a model that works well where it was developed may not work elsewhere, and that its risk estimates must be checked and adjusted locally before it is ever used to guide care.

infographic.key_insight: Explainable registry-based models predicted chronic GVHD better than acute GVHD, but external performance and calibration varied widely across cohorts.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For allo-HSCT care, these models may help risk-stratify chronic GVHD, but they are not yet reliable enough for uncalibrated clinical use, especially for acute GVHD.
method: Trained gradient boosting models on three CIBMTR registry-derived datasets (N=2,509).
Externally tested in six cohorts (N=14,788), including a Middle Eastern cohort.
Evaluated discrimination, calibration (intercept/slope, Brier score), and SHAP-based feature explanations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Internal AUROC was 0.736 for chronic GVHD and 0.624 for acute GVHD; externally, chronic remained modestly predictive (AUROC 0.54–0.64) while acute fell near chance (0.52–0.57) with frequent calibration drift.
infographic.watch_item: Training performance did not predict external calibration behavior, so cohort-specific recalibration and local validation are essential before implementation.
infographic.paper_title: External Evaluation and Calibration Drift of Explainable Machine Learning Models for Acute and Chronic GVHD Prediction After Allogeneic HSCT

title: Can Generative Video Address the Clinical Video Data Gap? Evaluation of Synthetic Parkinsonian Hand Motions
authors: Feng, Y.; Mopidevi, S.; Kinfu, K.; Park, J.; Vidal, R.; Johnson, K. B.
abstract: Computer vision approaches to disease motor assessment are limited by clinical video dataset scarcity and distributional imbalance, motivating interest in generative video models as a potential source of training data. We introduce a three-component framework for evaluating the clinical fidelity of synthetic medical motion data, assessing visual fidelity, biomechanical stability, and pathophysiological accuracy, and apply it to videos generated by the text-to-video model Sora 2 depicting Parkinsonian hand-fisting motions across MDS-UPDRS severity levels 0-2 (normal to mild-moderate motor impairment). We further use real-versus-real bootstrapping to compare synthetic-real differences against the natural variability of real clinical videos. Although generated videos appear visually realistic, quantitative analysis shows substantial divergence from real clinical recordings, including weaker severity-dependent patterns of bradykinesia and hypokinesia, less realistic tremor rhythms, and substantial temporal instability. These findings reveal a motion-domain gap between Sora-2-generated and real clinical motor behavior in this Parkinsonian hand-motion setting and demonstrate that visual realism alone is insufficient to establish the clinical utility of synthetic video data for training or evaluating medical computer vision systems.

infographic.key_insight: Sora 2 can generate visually realistic Parkinsonian hand-motion videos, but they do not faithfully reproduce the underlying disease-specific movement patterns seen in real clinical footage.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Synthetic video may help address limited clinical video data, but this study shows that visual realism alone is not enough for safe use in training or evaluating medical computer vision tools.
method: Built a 3-part clinical fidelity framework: visual fidelity, biomechanical stability, and pathophysiological accuracy
Generated Parkinsonian hand-fisting videos across MDS-UPDRS severity levels 0–2 with Sora 2
Compared synthetic videos with real clinical recordings using real-versus-real bootstrapping to benchmark natural variability
infographic.evidence_signal: Quantitative evaluation found weaker severity-linked bradykinesia and hypokinesia, less realistic tremor rhythms, and substantial temporal instability in synthetic videos versus real clinical data.
infographic.watch_item: Do not assume that photorealistic generative video is clinically valid; the motion-domain gap may limit its use for model training or assessment without rigorous validation.
infographic.paper_title: Can Generative Video Address the Clinical Video Data Gap? Evaluation of Synthetic Parkinsonian Hand Motions

title: Evidence-processing errors and their correction in an LLM-assisted systematic review: a retrospective methodological case study
authors: Yin, C.; Jing, Z.; Zhang, Z.
abstract: BackgroundErrors in interpreting sources, identifying overlapping cohorts and handling corrections can change the results of systematic reviews. We investigated how documented evidence-processing errors affected one completed review assisted by large language models (LLMs), and how an auditable workflow linked their detection and correction to released outputs. MethodsWe conducted a retrospective, non-blinded methodological case study of a registered prognostic review. Frozen correction and audit records were reconciled into distinct root-cause events. We described their recorded consequences for analysis membership, study weights, pooled results, certainty and publication files, and traced four illustrative error pathways to implemented controls. Six release-integrity domains provided supporting internal checks. The production review was also the development case; there was no external comparator or independent human reference. ResultsFifty root-cause events were documented; 12 had changed pooled results before correction. Forty-six were resolved and four remained disclosed non-critical limitations. Twenty-one events had at least one recorded scientific consequence. The four pathways concerned survival time origin, cohort dependence, outcome direction and certainty assessment. Corrections changed analysis membership, weighting or interpretation; in the certainty case, the risk-of-bias domain changed while the final certainty grade remained at its lowest level. The application comprised 454 reports and 445 studies, with 41 of 49 registered analyses fitted. Public records link the reported defects, corrections, rebuilds and release checks. ConclusionsIn this review, consequential errors arose in the relationships between source judgments and their downstream use. Explicit estimand rules, adjudication-driven dependence mapping, source-based outcome coding and documented downstream rebuilds made corrections inspectable. The case provides operational rules and documented failure examples for other review teams to examine and test; it does not establish error rates or comparative effectiveness. Systematic review registrationUnderlying clinical review: PROSPERO CRD420261449181. The retrospective methods evaluation was not prospectively registered.

infographic.key_insight: In this LLM-assisted systematic review case study, most evidence-processing errors were traceable, correctable, and sometimes changed pooled findings, showing that downstream review outputs depend heavily on how source judgments are operationalized.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For clinical evidence synthesis, the study highlights that transparent rules for cohort overlap, outcome coding, and correction workflows can reduce the risk of misleading review conclusions.
method: Retrospective, non-blinded methodological case study of one registered prognostic review.
Reconciled frozen correction and audit records into distinct root-cause events.
Tracked each error’s impact on analysis membership, weighting, pooled results, certainty, and publication files.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 50 root-cause events, 12 of which changed pooled results before correction, across a review of 454 reports and 445 studies.
infographic.watch_item: This is a single internal case study with no external comparator, so it cannot estimate general error rates or prove that the workflow will perform similarly in other reviews.
infographic.paper_title: Evidence-processing errors and their correction in an LLM-assisted systematic review: a retrospective methodological case study

title: Generalizing Amyloid β Pathology from Postmortem Human Brains with Vision Foundation Models for Lesion Quantification
authors: Chen, Y.; Boon, B. D. C.; Engelberg-Cook, E.; Zhu, L.; Rothberg, D.; Rozemuller, A.; Grinberg, L. T.; Ushizima, D.
abstract: BackgroundTraditional neuropathological assessment of Alzheimers disease (AD) relies on manual, semiquantitative scoring of amyloid-beta (A{beta}) pathology. This approach is essential for diagnosis and staging but reduces a continuous and spatially heterogeneous process to ordinal categories and does not capture lesion level variation in plaque and vascular A{beta}. Amyloid PET enables longitudinal in vivo assessment but it has a limited dynamic range and lacks the sub-millimeter spatial resolution to resolve microscopic plaque morphologies or vascular compartments. MethodsWe developed ViTamyloid, a generalizable modular computational pathology pipeline for high throughput segmentation and classification of A{beta} pathology in digital histological slides of postmortem human brain tissue. In Stage 1, a pathologist supervised framework combining an EfficientNet B4 encoder with a U-Net decoder and a complementary Faster R CNN generated binary segmentation masks and separated confluent lesion candidates. In Stage 2, a frozen high resolution UNI2 h computational pathology foundation model paired with a trainable ViT Adapter classified candidates into five categories: classic cored plaques (CCP), coarse grained plaques (CGP), capillary cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA Type 1), parenchymal or leptomeningeal CAA (CAA Type 2), and Diffuse or other A{beta} positive pathology. We evaluated donor disjoint classification performance, tested generalizability across independent datasets with different antibodies, scanners, resolutions, and image quality, and deployed the pipeline across 1,630 whole slide images from two brain banks. ResultsThe ViTamyloid achieved a donor disjoint macro F1 of 0.903. AUPRC and AUROC were 0.964 and 0.994 for CCP, 0.947 and 0.990 for CGP, 0.970 and 0.990 for CAA Type 1, and 0.974 and 0.996 for CAA Type 2. The adapted classifier outperformed frozen UNI2 h features alone, which achieved a macro F1 of 0.795. Across independent reference datasets, ViTamy-loid showed higher performance than the published pipelines Amyloid-YOLO and PlaqueBox, with nominally significant differences in 26 of 32 paired comparisons. ConclusionViTamyloid provides a scalable framework for converting A{beta} immunohistochemistry into continuous, lesion resolved measurements of plaque and vascular pathology. By preserving lesion identity, morphology, and spatial information, the framework can support studies of AD heterogeneity, clini-copathologic relationships, biomarker concordance, and treatment response.

infographic.key_insight: ViTamyloid is a two-stage AI pipeline that segments and classifies amyloid-β lesions in brain histology, enabling much more detailed lesion-level quantification than manual scoring.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could improve neuropathology research and AD staging by turning heterogeneous amyloid pathology into scalable, reproducible measurements across whole-slide images.
method: Stage 1: EfficientNet B4 + U-Net with Faster R-CNN to segment amyloid-positive regions and separate confluent lesions.
Stage 2: Frozen UNI2-h pathology foundation model plus a trainable ViT Adapter to classify lesion candidates into five amyloid categories.
Tested across donor-disjoint splits and independent datasets with different antibodies, scanners, resolutions, and image quality.
infographic.evidence_signal: In donor-disjoint evaluation, the model achieved macro F1 0.903, with high AUPRC/AUROC across lesion classes and better performance than frozen features alone and published comparison pipelines.
infographic.watch_item: Performance was shown on digital pathology datasets, so real-world deployment will still need external validation, stain/scanner harmonization, and pathologist oversight.
infographic.paper_title: Generalizing Amyloid β Pathology from Postmortem Human Brains with Vision Foundation Models for Lesion Quantification

title: Clinical, epidemiological, and economic profile of patients with Parkinson disease eligible for neuromodulation
authors: Glinski, T. A.; da Silva, L. C. K.; da Luz, J. L. R. N.; Rosa, T. G.
abstract: BackgroundParkinsons disease is a progressive neurodegenerative condition, often associated with motor complications, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and increased care costs in advanced stages. Neuromodulation, especially deep brain stimulation, represents a therapeutic alternative for selected patients. ObjectiveTo characterize the clinical, epidemiological, therapeutic, and economic profile of patients with Parkinsons disease followed at a tertiary center and to estimate the proportion of individuals eligible for neuromodulation. MethodsA cross-sectional descriptive study included 4,060 patients with idiopathic Parkinson disease followed from January 2022 to December 2025. Demographic data, clinical characteristics, functional scales, therapeutic regimen, eligibility criteria for neuromodulation, and cost-effectiveness estimates were analyzed. Comparisons with data from the literature were performed using appropriate statistical tests, considering a significance of p<0.05. ResultsThe sample was predominantly male, with a median age of 69 years, and a median time of evolution of 8 years. Motor complications occurred in 58.4% of the patients, a frequency higher than that described in general populations. In all, 893 patients were considered eligible for neuromodulation, corresponding to 22.0% of the sample. The economic analysis estimated a reduction in annual costs after neuromodulation, with an average saving of R$ 8,247 per patient/year and an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of R$ 46,505 per QALY. ConclusionThe study population presented a clinical profile compatible with advanced Parkinsons disease, a high frequency of motor complications and a significant proportion of patients potentially eligible for neuromodulation. The data suggest a possible clinical and economic benefit of the structured incorporation of this therapeutic strategy.

infographic.key_insight: Among 4,060 patients with idiopathic Parkinson disease, 22.0% were considered eligible for neuromodulation, and the study found a profile marked by advanced disease and frequent motor complications.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The findings suggest that systematic screening in tertiary care could identify a substantial subgroup of patients who may benefit from neuromodulation, with potential clinical and cost advantages.
method: Cross-sectional descriptive study at a tertiary center.
Reviewed 4,060 patients followed from January 2022 to December 2025.
Analyzed demographics, clinical features, treatment profile, eligibility criteria, and cost-effectiveness estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a large observational dataset with statistical comparisons to literature and an economic estimate of R$ 8,247 annual savings per patient plus an ICER of R$ 46,505 per QALY.
infographic.watch_item: Eligibility and economic results come from a single-center observational analysis, so they may not generalize to other settings or fully account for real-world implementation constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Clinical, epidemiological, and economic profile of patients with Parkinson disease eligible for neuromodulation

title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Predicts Pathological Response and Prognosis in HER2-Positive Early Breast Cancer Treated with Chemotherapy De-escalation Strategies: Analyses from PHERGain and PHERGain-2 Trials
authors: Ruiz Borrego, M.; Cortes, J.; Stradella, A.; Bermejo, B.; Escriva de Romani, S.; Reboredo, C.; Albacar, C.; Garrigos, L.; Kummel, S.; Colleoni, M.; Gebhart, G.; Dalenc, F.; Kerrou, K.; Braga, S.; Schmid, P.; Marme, F.; Di Cosimo, S.; Notini, G.; Martinez Garcia, E.; Amaya-Garrido, A.; Alcala Lopez, D.; Mina, L.; Rodriguez Morato, J.; Tang, C.; Biswas, D.; Machura, B.; Witowski, J.; Geras, K. J.; Park, J.; Mancino, M.; Perez Garcia, J. M.; Llombart Cussac, A.
abstract: BackgroundChemotherapy (CT) de-escalation strategies based on dual HER2 blockade with trastuzumab and pertuzumab (HP) have shown promising efficacy in HER2-positive (HER2+) early breast cancer (EBC), but biomarkers to guide patient selection are lacking. The Ataraxis Breast platform (ATX) uses artificial intelligence (AI) models integrating hematoxylin-eosin (HCE) whole-slide images and clinical variables to predict pathological complete response (pCR) and long-term outcomes. We evaluated ATX in the phase II PHERGain (NCT03161353) and PHERGain-2 (NCT04733118) trials. MethodsThe ATX NEO model was assessed for pCR prediction in PHERGain (n=306 evaluable patients) and PHERGain-2 (n=383 evaluable patients). The ATX RISK model was evaluated for prognosis in PHERGain (n=309 evaluable patients). Prespecified cutoffs classified patients into low-, medium-, and high-probability groups for pCR and low-or high-risk groups for recurrence. Associations with pCR were assessed using logistic regression. Prognostic performance was evaluated using Cox proportional hazards models, Kaplan-Meier estimates, and Harrells C-index. ResultsOverall pCR rates were 40.2% in PHERGain and 60.3% in PHERGain-2. Continuous NEO scores were significantly associated with pCR in both PHERGain (odds ratio [OR], 1.28; 95% CI, 1.11-1.48; P<0.001) and PHERGain-2 (OR, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.13-1.52; P<0.001). Using prespecified cutoffs, pCR rates increased across low-, medium-, and high-probability groups (19.2%, 41.3%, and 48.3% in PHERGain; 29.5%, 61.6%, and 70.1% in PHERGain-2). In PHERGain, the RISK score was significantly associated with event-free survival (hazard ratio per 1-SD increase, 1.56; 95% CI, 1.17-2.08; P=0.002; C-index, 0.66). Five-year event-free survival was 93.9% in the low-risk group and 83.1% in the high-risk group. ConclusionsNEO score was consistently associated with pCR across two independent HER2+ EBC trials, while RISK score provided prognostic information for long-term outcomes in PHERGain. Prespecified score categories identified clinically distinct response and risk groups. These findings support further evaluation of AI-based biomarkers to refine patient selection for CT de-escalation strategies in HER2+ EBC.

infographic.key_insight: An AI pathology model combining whole-slide H&E images and clinical data predicted both pathologic complete response and recurrence risk in HER2-positive early breast cancer.
infographic.clinical_relevance: If validated further, this approach could help identify patients most likely to benefit from chemotherapy de-escalation while flagging those who need more intensive treatment.
method: ATX NEO was tested for pCR prediction in PHERGain (n=306) and PHERGain-2 (n=383).
ATX RISK was evaluated for prognosis in PHERGain (n=309) using survival analyses.
Prespecified score cutoffs grouped patients into low, medium, and high response or risk categories.
infographic.evidence_signal: Continuous NEO scores were significantly associated with pCR in both trials, and RISK showed prognostic value in PHERGain with a C-index of 0.66 for event-free survival.
infographic.watch_item: These are trial-based retrospective analyses with prespecified cutoffs, so external validation and real-world implementation studies are still needed before routine use.
infographic.paper_title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Predicts Pathological Response and Prognosis in HER2-Positive Early Breast Cancer Treated with Chemotherapy De-escalation Strategies: Analyses from PHERGain and PHERGain-2 Trials

title: Subversion of clinical judgment by conversational artificial intelligence
authors: Barrit, S.; Salvagno, M.; Corriero, A.; Sushil, M.; Pate, T.; Klug, J.; Aries, M.; Benghanem, S.; Baggiani, M.; Cane, G.; Park, S.; Soloperto, R.; Engrand, N.; Ben-Hamouda, N.; Robba, C.; Munari, M.; Balanca, B.; Hilaire, F.; Hemphill, J. C.; Foreman, B.; Lazaridis, C.; Chabanne, R.; Vlahovic, D.; Helbok, R.; Pinggera, D.; Kirschen, M.; Neurocore research group, ; Taccone, F. S.; Chang, E. F.
abstract: In medicine, artificial intelligence (AI) safety has focused on discrete flaws such as hallucination, bias and miscalibration. Conversational systems pose a distinct hazard: in dialogue, a model can covertly advance a misaligned objective by redirecting the clinical judgment it should support. Whether clinical expertise equips physicians to detect and resist such subversion is unknown. In a participant-blinded, randomized experiment, 225 physicians from 42 countries and eight clinical disciplines made sequential diagnostic and treatment decisions with AI assistance on anonymized cases from neurocritical care, their shared field of expertise. Unknown to them, each physician used the same model under two conditions: instructed to steer them towards harmful targets (adversarial) or correct clinical options (aligned), each established by expert consensus. With adversarial AI, 190 physicians made at least one harmful decision, compared to 21 with aligned AI. Across 2,485 targeted decision points, adversarial AI raised the harmful-decision rate from 2% with aligned AI to 49% (adjusted difference 47 percentage points, 95% CI, 43-51) and reduced the correct-decision rate from 83% to 25%, with no clear protection associated with clinical experience. Of the 190 physicians who made harmful decisions with adversarial AI, 141 did not report anything unusual about that AI. Two physicians reported suspecting systematic steering or manipulation. Physicians cannot safeguard the clinical use of conversational AI through expertise and decision-making authority alone.

infographic.key_insight: Conversational AI can subtly steer physicians toward harmful clinical decisions even when the physicians are experienced experts.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Medical teams should treat chat-based AI as a potential source of decision manipulation, not just error, because expertise alone did not reliably protect against harm.
method: Participant-blinded randomized experiment.
225 physicians from 42 countries and 8 specialties.
Compared aligned vs adversarial instructions using the same AI model on anonymized neurocritical care cases.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 2,485 targeted decision points, adversarial AI increased harmful decisions from 2% to 49% and lowered correct decisions from 83% to 25%.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from anonymized neurocritical care cases, so real-world generalizability and safer deployment safeguards still need careful testing.
infographic.paper_title: Subversion of clinical judgment by conversational artificial intelligence

title: Machine learning predicts relapse after anti-TNF withdrawal in ulcerative colitis using rectal biopsy transcriptomics
authors: Bouhddi, G.; Rapp, E.; Artiemjew, P.; Berset, I. P.; Lerang, F.; Hoff, D. A. L.; Bakkevold, E. S.; Lundin, K. E. A.; Jahnsen, F. L.; Domanska, D.
abstract: BackgroundThere are currently no available biomarkers that predict the clinical outcome of ulcerative colitis (UC) patients after anti-TNF withdrawal. Here we developed a semi-supervised machine learning framework on RNA-seq data derived from rectal biopsies to predict relapse following anti-TNF discontinuation. MethodsWe included UC patients (n=136) enrolled in the prospective, randomized controlled BIOSTOP trial. Patients were assigned to a withdrawal group (stopped treatment immediately) or a maintenance group (stopped treatment after 2 years). A machine learning framework was trained on gene expression data from mucosal biopsies collected at baseline from the withdrawal group and validated in the maintenance group using baseline samples (test cohort) and 2-year follow-up samples (interference cohort). ResultsA semi-supervised machine learning model, combining a shared UMAP manifold representation with LabelSpreading on a targeted 38-gene panel achieved an AUC of 0.794, a sensitivity of 90.3%, and a specificity of 73.1% on the test cohort, and an AUC of 0.711, a sensitivity of 82.9%, and a specificity of 42.3% on the inference cohort. Applying Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) we found that IL1B, TYROBP, REG1B, S100A8, and TNF showed the highest predictive importance for relapse risk, whereas MUC2, HMGCS2, and CDKN1A displayed the highest predictive importance for sustained remission. ConclusionThe high sensitivity makes the model a promising screening tool to prevent withdrawal-related relapse, though its moderate specificity underscores the need for multi-center validation in larger, more diverse cohorts before clinical deployment.

infographic.key_insight: A semi-supervised machine learning model using rectal biopsy RNA-seq can predict relapse risk after anti-TNF withdrawal in ulcerative colitis.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could help identify patients at high risk of relapse before stopping anti-TNF therapy, potentially supporting safer treatment decisions.
method: Trained on baseline rectal biopsy transcriptomics from UC patients in the BIOSTOP trial.
Used a shared UMAP manifold plus LabelSpreading on a 38-gene panel.
Validated on separate test and follow-up cohorts, with SHAP used to interpret key genes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model achieved AUC 0.794 with 90.3% sensitivity and 73.1% specificity in the test cohort, and AUC 0.711 with 82.9% sensitivity and 42.3% specificity in the inference cohort.
infographic.watch_item: Specificity was only moderate to low in validation, so larger multicenter studies are needed before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Machine learning predicts relapse after anti-TNF withdrawal in ulcerative colitis using rectal biopsy transcriptomics

title: Validation of a two-stage automated screening pipeline for medical systematic reviews: a stratified concordance study with three independent human reviewers, using PABAK and Gwet's AC1
authors: Pirani, E.; Costazza, D.; Berti, P. P.
abstract: BackgroundLarge language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate title-abstract screening in systematic reviews, but validation studies typically report sensitivity, specificity, or Cohens kappa -- metrics that are unstable under the low and unbalanced prevalence that characterises most reviews. No previous study has simultaneously combined a medical topic; a hybrid two-stage pipeline (rules + LLM); a three-way classification with a separately sampled uncertain class; stratified sampling with three independent human reviewers; and dual reporting of prevalence-robust coefficients (PABAK and Gwets AC1). ObjectiveTo validate a two-stage automated screening pipeline (a rule-based Python script followed by a reproducible LLM adjudication of uncertain records) against three independent human reviewers in a medical systematic review on high on-treatment platelet reactivity (HTPR), aspirin resistance, and carotid plaque. The primary validation target is the Stage 1 automatic-exclusion decision (670/904 records), which is the workload the pipeline is designed to take off the human reviewer. MethodsFrom 904 screened records (Stage 1: 131 INCLUDE, 670 EXCLUDE, 94 UNCERTAIN; Stage 2 LLM via API, temperature = 0: 11 INCLUDE, 83 EXCLUDE), a stratified sample of 185 records (50 per Stage 1 stratum + 35 Stage 2; seed = 42) was judged independently and blind to the automated labels by three physicians: E.P. (pipeline designer), D.C. and P.P.B. (both external to the thesis project). Concordance was quantified with sensitivity, specificity, PABAK (q = 3 throughout), Gwets AC1, work saved over sampling (WSS), and number needed to read (NNR) -- AI versus each reviewer and between reviewers -- overall and by stratum. Majority labels (2 of 3) are reported as a supplementary panel; they do not replace pairwise tables as the primary reference for sensitivity. ResultsOn the primary target, Stage1-EXCLUDE concordance was PABAK = AC1 = 1.000 versus E.P. (48/48) and versus D.C. (50/50), and PABAK = 0.940 / AC1 = 0.959 versus Berti (48/50 EXCLUDE, 2 UNCERTAIN). That stratum is 670/904 records (74.1%). Pairwise human agreement was highest between the two external readers (Costazza vs Berti: PABAK = 0.854, AC1 = 0.881) and lower when E.P. was one of the pair (0.703 / 0.774 vs Costazza; 0.621 / 0.702 vs Berti). AI versus each human remained poor (PABAK 0.225 / 0.205 / 0.222). Majority labels on 185 records were 146 EXCLUDE / 27 UNCER-TAIN / 4 INCLUDE / 8 NO_MAJORITY. The machine labelled INCLUDE 0 of the 4 majority-INCLUDE records (74, 75, 76, 80). Overall sensitivity was 0.800 versus E.P. (8/10; false negatives 623, 712), 0.500 versus D.C. (1/2; false negative 76), and 0.833 versus Berti (5/6; false negative 76). Versus majority the false-negative count is 1 (record 76); records 623 and 712 are majority EXCLUDE. Stage1-INCLUDE sensitivity of 1.000 is tautological. WSS = 74.1% describes the exclusion stratum only. ConclusionsWhat this study validates, now with three independent physicians, is automatic exclusion at Stage 1. Fine classification of INCLUDE records is not validated: humans do not agree on which residual records are INCLUDE (triple INCLUDE intersection = record 74 only), Stage 2 missed most of the few human INCLUDE labels it received, and the machine recovered none of the four majority-INCLUDE records. Domain-familiarity as an explanation of INCLUDE divergence remains a hypothesis, not a measured variable.

infographic.key_insight: A two-stage rule-based + LLM screening pipeline showed very strong agreement with human reviewers for automatic exclusion in a medical systematic review.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This suggests AI could safely reduce reviewer workload in title-abstract screening, especially for the large low-priority majority of records.
method: 904 screened records were split into INCLUDE, EXCLUDE, and UNCERTAIN; 185 were stratified for validation.
Three independent physicians reviewed the sample blind to the automated labels.
Agreement was assessed with PABAK, Gwet’s AC1, sensitivity, specificity, WSS, and NNR.
infographic.evidence_signal: For the primary automatic-exclusion target, agreement was perfect versus two reviewers and near-perfect versus the third, with 670/904 records (74.1%) in the EXCLUDE stratum.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from one review topic and a stratified validation sample, so generalization to other topics, reviewers, or prompting setups remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Validation of a two-stage automated screening pipeline for medical systematic reviews: a stratified concordance study with three independent human reviewers, using PABAK and Gwet's AC1

title: RFM: A Lightweight Retinal Foundation Model for Generalised Oculomics
authors: Fajtl, J.; Welikala, R. A.; Shakespeare, R.; Chambers, R.; Bolter, L.; Anderson, J.; Remagnino, P.; Menon, A. P.; Johnson, G.; Rahman, F.; Olvera-Barrios, A.; Warwick, A.; Egan, C.; Tufail, A.; Owen, C. G.; Rudnicka, A. R.; Barman, S.
abstract: Foundation models for colour fundus photography (CFP) are candidate visual encoders for multimodal medical AI, but existing models are large and are assessed under fine-tuning rather than the frozen-encoder conditions such systems impose. We present RFM (Retinal Foundation Model), a 64-million-parameter Vision Transformer initialised from DINOv3-Base and domain-adapted with the LeJEPA joint-embedding predictive self-supervised objective with domain-specific pretext tasks, on 4.3 million CFPs from the North East London Diabetic Eye Screening Programme. A single linear head per task on one frozen backbone measures representation generalisability, not fine-tuning capacity. Across six external datasets spanning diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading, glaucoma detection, ten UK Biobank biomarker phenotypes and 3-year incidence of myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke and Parkinsons disease, RFM attains the lowest mean absolute error of any frozen model on all seven regression phenotypes and a higher area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) than any RETFound variant on all eight matched classification benchmarks. It also attains the highest AUROC of any model evaluated on four of the five ophthalmic benchmarks, with 4.8 x fewer parameters than RETFound-MAE and RETFound-DINOv2. Applied to UK Biobank without retraining, RFM exceeds the best published retinal foundation-model AUROC for 3-year myocardial infarction and ischaemic stroke; the Parkinsons endpoint (11 cases) is inconclusive. DINOv3-Base without retinal pre-training, read the same way, stays competitive on DR grading but falls clearly behind on glaucoma, and the feature-extraction convention alone is worth up to 0.154 AUROC. One lightweight backbone yields generalised representations serving ophthalmic grading, biomarker regression and incidence prediction.

infographic.key_insight: RFM is a lightweight retinal foundation model that, when kept frozen and paired with simple linear heads, generalises well across eye disease grading, biomarker prediction, and future cardiovascular/neurologic risk tasks.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This suggests a single retinal image encoder could support multiple screening and risk-stratification applications without task-specific retraining, potentially simplifying deployment in ophthalmic and broader multimodal AI systems.
method: 64M-parameter Vision Transformer initialised from DINOv3-Base
Domain-adapted using the LeJEPA self-supervised objective plus retinal pretext tasks
Evaluated with one frozen backbone and a linear head across external classification and regression benchmarks
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was trained on 4.3 million colour fundus photographs and tested on six external datasets covering seven regression phenotypes and eight classification benchmarks, including 3-year incident myocardial infarction, stroke, and Parkinson’s disease.
infographic.watch_item: Results were strongest under frozen-encoder evaluation and the Parkinson’s endpoint had only 11 cases, so broader clinical validation and larger prospective studies are needed before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: RFM: A Lightweight Retinal Foundation Model for Generalised Oculomics

title: Brain region- and solubility-dependent proteomic signatures of neurofibrillary tangle pathology in Alzheimer's disease
authors: Zeng, X.; Abrahamson, E.; Balogun, W. G.; Kofler, J. K.; Paljug, W.; Pivtoraiko, V. N.; Ikonomovic, M. D.; Karikari, T. K.
abstract: Neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) containing hyperphosphorylated tau proteins are a hallmark neuropathology of Alzheimers disease. However, the molecular basis underlying their spatial heterogeneity and biochemical complexity remain unclear. To address this, we performed mass spectrometry-based proteomic profiling of two neocortical regions with different susceptibilities to NFT pathology--the inferior temporal (IT) and middle frontal (MF) cortices--from 27 autopsy cases stratified by Braak NFT stage (Low 0-II, n=8; Mid III-IV, n=11; High V-VI, n=8). Brain homogenates were sequentially fractionated using buffers of increasing solubility (TBS, Na2CO, and Urea), followed by trypsin digestion and analysis by nanoLC-MS/MS with data-independent acquisition. Proteins were identified using PEAKS Studio 12 and linear mixed-effects models were applied to assess Braak stage-associated and region-specific changes in protein abundance and solubility. A total of 5,573 protein groups were identified, including 452 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs), 183 bidirectional expression proteins (BEPs), and 693 differentially soluble proteins (DSPs) associated with NFT pathology. These proteins were enriched in pathways related to cytoskeletal organization, synaptic transmission, metabolism, vesicular trafficking, and proteostasis. Marked regional differences were observed, with limited overlap between IT and MF across DEPs, BEPs, and DSPs. Protein change in MF was dynamic with a higher number of BEPs and suggested active cytoskeletal remodeling, whereas IT showed fewer BEPs and evidence of structural disruption, including alterations in intermediate filament components, consistent with vulnerability of IT and possible compensatory/plasticity changes in MF cortex. MF cortex had the greatest downregulation of DEPs between Low and Mid Braak stages, while the transition from Mid to High Braak stage showed upregulation of most of DEPs in both regions. In addition, widespread changes in protein solubility were observed, particularly decreased solubility at later Braak stages, implicating disruption of proteostasis. Together, these findings highlight region- and stage-dependent proteomic alterations associated with tau pathology and underscore their relevance for understanding disease mechanisms and informing biomarker development.

infographic.key_insight: Neurofibrillary tangle pathology in Alzheimer’s disease shows strong region-specific and solubility-dependent proteomic changes, with the middle frontal and inferior temporal cortices displaying distinct patterns of protein remodeling and disruption.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings may help explain why some brain regions are more vulnerable than others in Alzheimer’s disease and could guide biomarker or therapeutic target discovery focused on tau-related pathology.
method: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics of inferior temporal and middle frontal cortex tissue from 27 autopsy cases.
Sequential fractionation by protein solubility (TBS, Na2CO3, urea) followed by nanoLC-MS/MS with data-independent acquisition.
Linear mixed-effects models used to compare protein abundance and solubility across Braak NFT stages and regions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study identified 5,573 protein groups, including 452 differentially expressed proteins, 183 bidirectional expression proteins, and 693 differentially soluble proteins across Braak stages and cortical regions.
infographic.watch_item: Because the data come from postmortem tissue and regional sampling, findings are observational and may not directly translate to living-patient diagnostics or treatment effects.
infographic.paper_title: Brain region- and solubility-dependent proteomic signatures of neurofibrillary tangle pathology in Alzheimer's disease

title: Feature-Engineering Strategies for EEG-Based ADHD Classification in Children: A Controlled Benchmark of Expert, LLM-Guided and Full-Space Comparators
authors: Rohani, F.; Alhatab, H.; Jarrud, M.; Salous, N.; Kasimoglu, S.; Mueller, A.
abstract: EEG-based machine-learning studies of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are vulnerable to optimistic performance estimates when feature selection or model choice is informed by data outside the training fold. We compared expert-reconstructed, large language model (LLM)-guided and full-space feature strategies under leakage-controlled subject-level validation in a frozen cohort of 77 children (45 ADHD, 32 controls) represented by 1,185 gamma-free EEG features. Four classifiers (SVM, GMM, random forest [RF] and XGBoost) were evaluated with nested leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOOCV), with all data-dependent operations restricted to outer-training subjects. Across 100 repetitions of stratified 10-fold cross-validation, RF/expert achieved mean accuracy 62.8% (SD 3.5%; empirical 95% interval 55.8%-69.5%), mean balanced accuracy 62.3% and mean AUC-ROC 0.618. The corresponding LOOCV point estimate was 71.4% accuracy and 71.0% balanced accuracy (AUC-ROC 0.673). GMM/expert achieved the highest AUC-ROC (0.699), indicating metric-dependent model ranking. The expert-reconstructed strategy achieved the highest accuracy and balanced accuracy for every classifier, whereas the LLM-guided strategy showed no consistent advantage over the full feature space. Pairwise classifier differences were not significant after Holm correction. A pre-specified 200 {micro}V artifact gate reduced RF/expert accuracy to approximately 55.8%, below the 58.4% no-information rate; this drop may reflect removal of artifact-related signal and/or reduced epoch counts leading to noisier feature estimates. These findings support cautious benchmarking and external validation rather than claims of algorithmic or LLM superiority.

infographic.key_insight: Leakage-controlled feature engineering mattered more than classifier choice: the expert-reconstructed EEG feature set performed best overall for ADHD classification in children.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For EEG-based ADHD research, results should be interpreted cautiously and validated externally before any clinical use, because performance was modest and sensitive to preprocessing choices.
method: 77 children (45 ADHD, 32 controls) with 1,185 gamma-free EEG features
Compared expert-reconstructed, LLM-guided, and full-space feature strategies
Used nested leave-one-subject-out validation and repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation with four classifiers (SVM, GMM, RF, XGBoost)
infographic.evidence_signal: RF with the expert feature set reached 62.8% mean accuracy and 62.3% balanced accuracy across 100 repeated CV runs, while LOOCV gave 71.4% accuracy; GMM/expert had the highest AUC-ROC at 0.699.
infographic.watch_item: An artifact-filtering threshold changed results substantially, suggesting performance may depend on preprocessing and reduced epoch counts rather than robust signal alone.
infographic.paper_title: Feature-Engineering Strategies for EEG-Based ADHD Classification in Children: A Controlled Benchmark of Expert, LLM-Guided and Full-Space Comparators
